chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Faddal, he raised it to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
"The wedding feast (walimah) for one or two days is an act of honor, but for three days it is showing off and seeking fame."

key_terms.اَلْوَلِيمَةُ: The wedding feast or banquet hosted by the groom's family
key_terms.رِيَاءٌ: Showing off or performing deeds for the sake of being seen by others
key_terms.سُمْعَةٌ: Seeking fame, reputation, or public acclaim
key_terms.مَكْرُمَةٌ: An act of honor or generosity

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on the duration of wedding feasts to avoid showing off?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) establishes a clear ethical boundary in wedding celebrations, framing the one-to-two-day feast as an act of honor (makrumah) while identifying the three-day extension as a potential trap for ostentation (riya') and public acclaim (sum'ah). This distinction reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on balancing social generosity with spiritual sincerity, warning against the social pressure to prolong festivities beyond necessity for the sake of status. The hadith thus serves as a practical guideline for maintaining modesty in communal rituals, ensuring that the celebration remains a sincere act of worship rather than a display of wealth.
